hook: The monk who walked from China to India and back to find the true teachings of the Buddha.

pages.x: Xuanzang became a Buddhist monk at 13, in Luoyang, and soon found that the Chinese translations of the Buddhist books were muddled and contradicted each other. He decided to go to India, the land of the Buddha, and bring back the originals.

The Tang emperor had banned travel abroad, but in 629 Xuanzang slipped out anyway, travelling by night. Crossing the Gobi Desert alone, he spilled his water bag and went five days without water, until his old horse led him to a spring.

pages.t: Across the roof of the world
pages.x: He crossed the icy Tian Shan mountains, where many of his companions froze to death, and passed through Samarkand and Bamiyan, with its giant stone Buddhas, then over the Khyber Pass into India.

In India he spent years at Nalanda, the greatest university of the age, with thousands of monks, and visited the places where the Buddha had lived and taught. He debated so brilliantly that King Harsha held a great assembly in his honour.

He came back to Chang'an in 645, sixteen years after leaving, with 657 Buddhist texts carried by 20 horses. The emperor forgave him and asked him to write about his travels. He spent the rest of his life translating, and the Big Wild Goose Pagoda was built to keep his books.

Nine centuries later his journey inspired Journey to the West, one of China's best-loved novels, in which a monk travels to India guarded by the Monkey King, a pig and a river spirit. It has been retold in countless films, cartoons and games.

Xuanzang's translations shaped Chinese Buddhism, and his account of his travels is still a key source on old Central Asia and India; archaeologists used it to find lost Buddhist sites, Nalanda among them.
pts: Travelled 16 years to India and back
Inspired the novel Journey to the West
